title: The Economics of Falling Net FDI in India
description: Context: A comprehensive economic analysis highlights a structural contraction in India’s net Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), which dropped from its historic peak of $44.0 billion in FY21 to less than $1.0 billion in FY25, before recovering mildly to $7.6 billion in FY26. About The Economics of Falling Net FDI in India: Key Data and Statistics on India’s FDI Performance: The Imperative Need to Deeply Analyze Net FDI Declines: Example: Financial investors (PE/VC funds, sovereign wealth funds) now command a massive 40.5% share of effective inflows, matching traditional Real FDI at 41.9%. Example: Internal reorganizations, share swaps, and ECB conversions accounted for $40 billion of the $560 billion equity inflows between 2014-15 and 2025-26. Example: A major 45% of India’s $65 billion outbound capital went into holding companies and SPVs in financial hubs like Singapore and the UAE. Initiatives and Policy Tools Deployed So Far: Key Institutional Challenges and Blind Spots: Example: Singapore’s Temasek exited Schneider Electric India in 2025, turning an initial $637 million investment into a $6.4 billion cash payout. Example: Diaspora and SPV flows account for 17.6% of effective inflows, often involving recycled Indian capital passing through offshore centers. Example: Attributable IPR and royalty payments alone drained $46.6 billion out of the country between 2022-23 and 2025-26. India’s impressive gross FDI figures hide a fragile financial reality where capital is exiting the country significantly faster than fresh productive investment is arriving. By focusing on headline numbers, policymakers miss the systemic slowdown in long-term manufacturing investment and the rise of short-term financial exits. Underline the reasons behind the recent decline in India’s net FDI inflows. Analyse the role of outward FDI and disinvestment trends. Suggest measures to realign FDI with domestic capital formation and industrial growth. (15 M)

title: Securing India Against the Threat of a 'Mythocalypse'
description: GS Paper III – Security (Cyber Security) | GS Paper III – Science & Technology Frontier AI; Cyber Vulnerabilities; Critical Infrastructure; AI Safety Institute; Defensive AI Recent advances in AI-powered cybersecurity, exemplified by Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, have enabled the discovery of complex vulnerabilities that often escape human experts and conventional testing. Its ability to autonomously combine minor flaws into major attack pathways highlights emerging security risks. With only a small fraction of identified vulnerabilities patched, India must rapidly strengthen its cyber resilience and governance architecture to stay ahead of evolving AI-driven threats. Why Mythos is Different and More Dangerous Advanced AI systems are rapidly transforming cybersecurity by identifying vulnerabilities beyond human capability and autonomously combining minor flaws into major attack vectors. While India possesses strong digital public infrastructure, legacy backend systems, workforce shortages, and the absence of a dedicated AI safety framework expose critical risks. India must urgently strengthen AI governance, cyber resilience, and international cooperation to stay ahead of emerging AI-driven threats. https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/lead/securing-india-against-the-threat-of-a-mythocalypse/article71081835.ece

title: Recalibrating the India-Bangladesh Partnership
description: This editorial is based on “The trust deficit in India-Bangladesh ties” published in The Hindu on 09/06/2026. The article emphasizes that unresolved issues—including asylum for Sheikh Hasina, border management disputes, and water-sharing—are stalling cooperation, necessitating a shift toward public-centric diplomacy. For Prelims: Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), Least Developed Country (LDC), India-Bangladesh Friendship Pipeline, Maitree Super Thermal Power Plant, Lines of Credit (LoCs), Teesta, Ganges, BIMSTEC,BBIN (Bangladesh-Bhutan-India-Nepal) Motor Vehicles Agreement, 1996 Ganges Water Treaty, Teesta River dispute, 2015 Land Boundary Agreement (LBA). For Mains: Areas of convergence and divergence between India and Bangladesh, Steps needed to strengthen India-Bangladesh bilateral relations. The bilateral relationship between India and Bangladesh remains in a state of diplomatic paralysis more than 100 days into the Tarique Rahman administration (Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)), characterized by mutual expectations that remain unaddressed. Despite high-level Indian outreach (including visits by the External Affairs Minister and the participation of the Lok Sabha Speaker in the swearing-in ceremony of the new Bangladeshi PM), Dhaka views these gestures as insufficient without the reversal of restrictive measures imposed during the previous interim government.
